overview.intro: Section B’s creative writing component carries 16 of its 23 marks across four short and long tasks: a classified advertisement up to 50 words, a poster up to 50 words, a speech of 120–150 words and a debate of 120–150 words, each attempted one out of two. Every task is marked on a stated split of format, content and expression, which makes this the most predictable part of the paper — if you know what the format demands, a large share of the marks is structural rather than inspired. This unit teaches the four formats precisely, then the language habits the expression marks reward.

learningOutcomes: Produce a classified advertisement within the word limit with every required detail.
Design a poster that carries heading, contents and issuing body in the given space.
Write a speech with an address, an argument and a peroration.
Write a debate speech that states a position, argues it and anticipates rebuttal.
Apply the format–content–expression split deliberately to each task.

learn.title: The two short tasks: advertisement and poster

blocks.text: A classified advertisement is a transaction reduced to essentials. The format mark is for the layout a newspaper would use: a heading naming the category — WANTED, FOR SALE, LOST AND FOUND, SITUATION VACANT — and then the details arranged so a reader can act. For a sale, the item, its condition, the price and the mode of contact; for a situation vacant, the post, the qualifications required, the salary offered and how to apply; for a lost item, the description, the place and time of loss, and a contact. Within fifty words every one of those must appear, which means no opening sentence, no adjectives beyond one and no pleasantries.

The poster is read from a distance, so its format mark follows hierarchy: a heading in capitals or a bold line that states the subject, the contents — what, when, where, who it is for — in a legible order, and the issuing authority at the foot, because a poster without a source is not credible. Fifty words again forces selection: the four questions a reader asks (what is it, when, where, whom do I contact) must all be answered. Content marks go to completeness of those particulars; expression marks go to clarity and economy, so telegraphic phrasing is not merely permitted but expected.

learn.title: Speech: 120–150 words with Format 1, Content 2, Expression 2

blocks.text: A speech is written to be heard, and the format mark recognises its three conventional parts. Open by addressing the audience — “Respected Principal, teachers and dear friends” — and state the occasion in the first two sentences, because a listener cannot reread. The body develops two or three points in short paragraphs, each announced before it is made, since a hearing audience follows signposts. The close is a peroration: a return to the theme in one strong sentence and a call to action or a wish, followed by “Thank you”.

Content’s two marks come from developing the given topic with specific, relevant material rather than restating the prompt, and from keeping the three or four points distinct. Expression’s two marks reward the qualities of spoken prose: contractions and natural rhythm are acceptable, rhetorical questions and repetition in threes are welcome, but clichés and purple language are not, and nothing may be so colloquial that it would embarrass the speaker. The word limit of 120–150 allows roughly four short paragraphs: address and introduction, two development paragraphs, and the close.

blocks.caption: Speech structure in four moves
rows: Expression: a strong final line and a call to action

blocks.text: The debate speech differs from the speech in having a side. The format mark is for the conventional opening — “I stand for/against the motion” or “I strongly agree/disagree with the statement” — stated in the first line, followed by a thesis sentence that gives your position in one clear claim. A debate that has not declared its side by the end of its first paragraph has already surrendered the format mark.

Content then requires argument rather than assertion: two reasons, each with a fact, an example or a reasoned consequence, is the reliable shape for 150 words. The third element that distinguishes a strong debate speech is anticipation of rebuttal — one sentence naming the opposing argument and answering it — because that is what marks the difference between a speech and an essay read aloud. Expression rewards the register of reasoned advocacy: confident modals, connectives that mark concession (“while it is true that…”), and a final sentence that returns to the motion. Watch the topical framing the question provides and stay inside it: content marks are lost to arguments about a neighbouring issue.

items: Declare the side in the first line; the thesis follows immediately.
Two reasons with support beat four reasons asserted.
Name and answer the strongest opposing argument in one sentence.
Stay on the exact motion given; neighbouring issues cost content marks.
Close by returning to the motion, not by trailing off.

learn.title: Expression marks and how to spend time

blocks.text: Expression is the mark category students treat as mystery and examiners treat as consistency. It rewards four things: staying within the word limit, grammatical accuracy, a register appropriate to the format, and sentences that carry one idea each. Within a word limit, brevity is scored favourably — a 130-word piece that says one thing well beats a 150-word piece that says three badly — because the examiner reads for fluency and economy together.

Timing matters because these 16 marks arrive in a section that also carries the 7 grammar marks, and both are quicker to earn than literature’s 31. Attempt one question from each pair, as instructed: attempting both wastes time on duplicates and invites exceeding limits. A workable discipline is to plan the longer pieces in five word-marks — audience, occasion, two points, close — before writing, since a speech that discovers its ending at word 148 will not have a peroration, and the peroration carries the expression marks.

keyPoints: Four tasks carry 16 marks: advertisement 3, poster 3, speech 5, debate 5.
Each task is attempted one out of two questions.
The advertisement needs a category heading and every transactional detail.
The poster needs hierarchy: heading, particulars, issuing authority.
The speech needs address, occasion, developed points and a peroration.
The debate needs the side declared first, two supported reasons and a rebuttal.
Content marks reward the required particulars, not extra material.
Expression marks reward the word limit, accuracy, register and economy.
Plan the long pieces in stages before writing; the close carries expression marks.
These 16 marks arrive faster than the literature section’s 31.
examFocus: Write the heading or the declaration first — it is a mark, not a decoration.
Count words in short tasks: one word over loses the limit’s credibility.
In speech and debate, the last sentence is graded: end on a return to the topic.
Attempt one question from each pair, as the paper instructs.
Register must suit the format: a poster is telegraphic, a debate is reasoned.

questions.prompt: A classified advertisement of up to 50 words carries:
questions.explanation: Format 1, content 1 and expression 1 make 3 marks for the advertisement task.

questions.prompt: The element that earns the format mark in a speech is:
options: The address, the statement of occasion and the peroration
questions.answer: The address, the statement of occasion and the peroration
questions.explanation: Format rewards the conventional structure: audience addressed, occasion stated, points signposted and a close.

questions.prompt: In a debate speech, the first line should:
options: Declare which side of the motion the speaker stands on
questions.answer: Declare which side of the motion the speaker stands on
questions.explanation: The side must be declared immediately; failing to declare it surrenders the format mark.

questions.prompt: A 150-word speech that lists four points without developing any of them is likely to lose marks chiefly in:
questions.explanation: Content requires developed, specific material and expression rewards one idea carried per sentence; a list satisfies neither.

questions.prompt: The concluding passage of a speech that restates the theme forcefully is the __________ .
questions.explanation: The close carries expression marks, so it must be planned rather than improvised at the word limit.

questions.prompt: A sentence in a debate that names the opposing argument and answers it is a __________ .
questions.explanation: Anticipating and answering the strongest opposing point is what distinguishes a debate speech from an essay read aloud.

questions.prompt: State the details that a classified advertisement must contain for an item offered for sale.
questions.answer: For an item offered for sale, the advertisement must contain: the category heading such as FOR SALE; the item itself described briefly; its condition; the price demanded; and the mode of contact — a telephone number, an address or a time at which the seller may be reached. The whole must stay within fifty words, which excludes any opening sentence or pleasantries. For a situation vacant the equivalents are the post, qualifications required, salary and how to apply, and for a lost item the description, the place and time of loss and a contact.
questions.explanation: The required particulars must be listed as particulars, and the word limit acknowledged.

questions.prompt: How does a debate speech differ from an ordinary speech on the same topic?
questions.answer: An ordinary speech addresses an audience on a topic and develops it as the speaker thinks best; its format mark comes from the address, the statement of occasion, signposted points and a peroration. A debate speech is bound to one side of a motion, so its first line must declare that side and its thesis sentence must state the position as a claim, which is what the format mark is attached to. In content, the ordinary speech may range freely while the debate speech must choose reasons that support its side and must anticipate the opposing argument — one sentence naming the strongest objection and answering it — because rebuttal is what marks advocacy rather than narration. Its expression register is reasoned advocacy rather than ceremony: confident modals, concession markers such as “while it is true that”, and a close that returns to the motion rather than to thanks alone.
questions.explanation: Three differences must be given — declaration, content selection with rebuttal, and register — each tied to where the marks sit.

questions.prompt: Explain how the format–content–expression marking split should be used while planning each writing task.
questions.answer: The split is a planning instrument, because each of the three categories rewards a different decision and each is marked separately. Format is decided first and costs almost nothing once the template is known: for the advertisement, the category heading and the arrangement of particulars; for the poster, the hierarchy of heading, contents and issuing authority; for the speech, the address and occasion at the opening and the peroration at the close; for the debate, the declaration of the side in the first line. Because format is worth one mark in every task, a piece with wrong format is capped immediately, so the template should be laid out before any sentence is written. Content is decided next and carries the larger share in the long tasks: it requires every particular the question demands and no material from a neighbouring topic, developed rather than asserted — which in the speech and debate means two points with support rather than four points named. In the short tasks content is completeness, since fifty words will hold exactly the required particulars. Expression is judged last and rewards constraints rather than ornament: staying inside the word limit, grammatical accuracy, a register that suits the genre, and one idea to a sentence. Planning should therefore proceed in that order — template, required content, then wording — with a word budget allocated to each part before writing: roughly fifteen words for a short task’s particulars, and for the long tasks about twenty for the opening, thirty to forty for each development paragraph and twenty-five for the close. The practical consequence is that the expression marks, which students treat as a matter of style, are mostly won by planning: a piece that knows where it ends will not overrun, will not lose its close, and will read as one connected whole.
questions.explanation: Full marks need the three categories mapped to planning decisions, the word-budget approach, and the point that expression is largely a planning outcome.

questions.prompt: Are these writing tasks testing writing ability or memory for formats? Discuss.
questions.answer: The case that they test memory is strong. Each task has a fixed word limit, a fixed mark split and a fixed set of required particulars, and the format mark — one of three, one of five — is explicitly for layout rather than for invention. An advertisement with the right heading and all its details scores whether or not its prose is elegant; a speech with an address, signposted points and a close scores its structure before it scores anything else. The prescribed topics are conventional, and a student who has learned four templates can reproduce them under examination conditions, which is why model-answer practice appears to raise scores so quickly. The case that real ability is being tested rests on the other two-thirds. Content marks require selecting what a particular audience needs from a particular prompt, and the fifty-word limit forces exactly the judgement that distinguishes competent writers: what may be cut without losing the transaction. Expression marks in the longer tasks reward connectedness — one idea to a sentence, a register that suits a hearing audience, a peroration that lands — which no template supplies, since templates are what students write when they cannot yet hear the difference between a sentence that carries and a sentence that fills. The debate’s rebuttal is the clearest evidence: naming and answering the opposing argument is a rhetorical act, not a format element, and it appears precisely where advocacy becomes real. The balanced judgement is that the tasks are deliberately pitched at the point where format and ability overlap: format guarantees a floor of marks for prepared students, while content and expression discriminate among them, and the mark split encodes that design — one mark for the frame, the rest for what is done inside it. Practically, both readings give the same advice: learn the formats until they are free, then spend the preparation on selection and sentence-level control, because that is where the remaining marks are decided.
questions.explanation: Full marks require the format argument with evidence from the mark split, the counter-argument using content, expression and rebuttal, and a judgement about what the design intends.
